title: Fast path and allocations
sub: When await costs nothing, and what still lands on the heap
cards/0/body:
If the awaited task has already completed (a cache hit, data already in a buffer), its awaiter answers IsCompleted = true. Then, inside MoveNext:

  • 1. the subscribe branch is skipped: state isn't written and there's no return;
  • 2. GetResult is called right away and hands over the ready result;
  • 3. the same MoveNext call keeps going to the next await.

No subscription, no leaving the method, no thread switch, and the state machine stays on the stack. This is the fast path.
cards/1/task: The results are already ready. Walk the fast path and watch the if (!awaiter.IsCompleted) line: does MoveNext ever reach the return inside it?
cards/2/q: A handler called SumAsync, and both tasks inside have already completed. Which thread runs return a + b?
cards/2/options/0: The one that called SumAsync: the method ran straight through in the first MoveNext call
cards/2/options/2: Whichever thread once completed the GetBAsync task
cards/2/explain: There were no pauses, so there are no continuations either: builder.Start ran the whole method on the caller's thread.
cards/3/body:
A pause usually costs one allocation: the state machine moves to the heap, and that box is the task itself (previous lesson).

The fast path keeps the machine on the stack. But the caller still needs a task object, and the result has to live somewhere. So an async Task<int> that returned 1000 without a single pause still creates a new Task<int>.

The exception is values for which .NET keeps ready-made completed tasks: true and false, ints from −1 to 8, and the default value (null, 0, 0.0…). Task.FromResult(x) gives you the same completed task with result x by hand, and in modern .NET it uses the same cache: for 5 or null it returns a shared object, for 1000 a new one.
cards/3/code:
Task<int>  a = CountAsync();       // returned 1000 without a pause → a new Task<int>
Task<int>  b = CountAsync();       // and another one: ReferenceEquals(a, b) == false
Task<bool> c = CheckAsync();       // returned true → a shared completed task from the cache
Task<int>  d = Task.FromResult(5); // 5 is within −1…8 → also from the cache
cards/4/body:
These create no heap objects at all:

  • Task.CompletedTask, a single shared completed task with no result;
  • an async Task with no result that finished without a pause: the builder hands out that same shared task;
  • an async Task<T> that returned a cached value (true, false, −1…8, default);
  • a ValueTask<T> with a ready value: it's a struct, and the result lives right inside it.
cards/4/code:
// the method finished without a single pause: what landed on the heap?
async Task           SaveAsync()  { … }  // nothing: the shared completed task
async Task<bool>     CheckAsync() { … }  // nothing: tasks for true/false exist in advance
async Task<int>      CountAsync() { … }  // returned 1000 → a new Task<int>
async ValueTask<int> PeekAsync()  { … }  // nothing: the result is in the struct itself
cards/5/q: async Task<int> CountAsync() found the value in a cache and returned 1000 without a single pause. What ended up on the heap?
cards/5/options/0: Only a Task<int> object holding the result; the state machine stayed on the stack
cards/5/options/1: Nothing: without a pause an async method allocates no memory
cards/5/options/2: Both the state machine and a Task<int>
cards/5/explain: The machine moves to the heap only on a pause. But the caller needs a task with result 1000, and there's no ready-made one in the cache.
cards/6/q: What creates no new heap objects? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/2: await on an already completed task
cards/6/options/3: An async Task<int> that returned 1000 without a pause
cards/6/explain: CompletedTask is a shared object, ValueTask is a struct, and awaiting a finished task takes the fast path. A Task<int> holding 1000 is a new object, and a pause puts the machine on the heap.
cards/7/q: A method reads a cache, and the data is there 99% of the time. What should it return so that a cache hit allocates nothing?
cards/7/options/0: ValueTask<T>: on a cache hit the result lives in the struct
cards/7/options/1: async Task<T>: since the await doesn't pause, there are no allocations anyway
cards/7/explain: async Task<T> creates a new Task<T> on every hit (except for cached values). A ValueTask<T> with a ready value doesn't touch the heap.
cards/8/q: Which line is the allocation-free fast path?
cards/8/explain: A ValueTask with a ready value is a struct, so the heap isn't touched. The last line wraps the real LoadUserAsync task.
cards/9/body:
ValueTask pays for the savings with rules. It's single-use: behind it there may be an object that gets reused for another operation after the first await. So you await a ValueTask exactly once and never from two places at the same time. If you need more, turn it into an ordinary task first with .AsTask().

Hence the rule of thumb: Task<T> by default. ValueTask when the method is called very often, usually completes right away, and the profiler has shown the allocations.
cards/9/deep: Since .NET 6 you can mark a method with [AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))], and then even a ValueTask method that suspends takes its objects from a pool. Turn it on selectively and after measuring.
cards/10/q: Can you await the same ValueTask twice?
cards/10/options/0: No: the behavior is undefined; if you need it more than once, call .AsTask() first
cards/10/explain: A ValueTask is single-use: there may be a reused object behind it. Only a Task can be awaited many times.
cards/11/pairs/0/1: A shared completed task with no result
cards/11/pairs/1/1: A completed task with a result
cards/11/pairs/2/1: No allocation on the fast path
